thesis: This is an exit instruction for the open 2026-08-24 long at 132.00, not a new idea. thesis: Exit instruction for the open long at 199.00, and the reason is arithmetic rather than fear. RTX ATR14 is 5.90, so the standing 186.00 stop is exactly 1.00 ATR from the 191.88 close against a 2.00 ATR swing floor — it will be taken out by an ordinary session. Moving it to a compliant 180.00 makes the trade 19.00 of risk against 27.50 of reward to the 226.50 target, a 1.45 ratio that is below the 2.0 floor. There is no version of this position that carries both a real stop and a publishable reward-to-risk, and the rule is that an idea needing a tight stop to clear the floor has failed the floor. The thesis separately took a dated, quantified hit two days after entry: the White House FY2027 request is $1.5T, the Democratic House proposal is about $1.15T, and Jefferies expects the outcome nearer the House number.
key_risk: Selling the name the market has already singled out as the least exposed. RTX fell only ~3% on 2026-11-04 against LMT -6.9% and LHX -6%+, and on 2026-11-05 it fell 3.30% against SPY -4.41% — it outperformed both the election and the crash, because roughly half the company is commercial aerospace that no appropriations bill touches.
counter_argument: The strongest case for holding is exactly that outperformance plus the commercial aftermarket, and UBS putting a ~$1.1T base budget inside the range of acceptable outcomes. It does not survive the stop question: keeping the position means keeping a 1.0-ATR stop, which is the single characteristic shared by all ten of this report first-month stop-outs. Closing and re-entering later at a workable level is a separate trade and is allowed.

thesis: This amends the exits on the open 2026-10-12 long at 262.00; the entry is filled and does not move. HII gapped from 279.26 to 316.21 on 2026-10-29 on earnings, held a 296.51-322.56 base for four sessions, then broke it — 303.99 on 11-04 and 289.41 on 11-05, down 8.7% in two sessions as the defence complex repriced. The position has never carried a stop, which was tolerable at 262 and is not tolerable at +10.5% with a sector headwind. Why HII and not RTX: shipbuilding sits in the lines a contested budget protects. Analysts expect bipartisan support for China deterrence and nuclear modernisation, which is the Virginia-class and Columbia-class and carrier work, while the Iran- and Israel-related lines are where the cuts are expected. HII is also the only prime whose backlog is measured in decades of hull construction rather than in annual procurement.
key_risk: The FY2027 budget gap is real and large — a $1.5T request against a ~$1.15T House proposal — and no budget is finalised, so the overhang persists for months with no scheduled resolution. HII is also thin for a prime at $172.5M average daily dollar volume, and it is 37% below its 460.00 high, so the chart is a downtrend with one earnings gap in it, not a recovery.
counter_argument: The case for closing alongside RTX is that both are defence primes facing the same appropriations risk and HII fell harder on the crash day. Answered on the composition of the cut rather than on the headline: the programmes expected to survive are nuclear and China-facing, which is what HII builds, whereas RTX effects-and-munitions exposure sits in the lines analysts name as vulnerable. The difference is also why HII can carry a 2.05 ATR stop that still locks the trade green while RTX cannot carry one at all.

catalyst.event: Tax-free separation into two independent public companies, announced in the 2026-11-04 8-K, targeted for completion by 2028 — retail pharmacy split from Aetna and Caremark. The driver is the re-rating of the remaining insurance-plus-PBM business, not a dated print
catalyst.action: accumulate in thirds across the 76-82 zone; the first third at 79 or better, add under 76, keep the last third for a PBM-legislation headline. No rush — the separation runs to 2028

thesis: CVS fell 12.5% on 2026-11-04 to 79.96 and closed 81.33 on 11-05, and it did so on an announcement rather than on a disappointment: the same day it beat Q3 consensus by 25.4% and raised its outlook. Trailing twelve-month EPS is 2.09 + 2.58 + 2.57 + 1.09 = 8.33, so at 81.33 the stock trades at 9.8x earnings it has beaten by 8.8%, 15.8%, 38.0% and 25.4% in four consecutive quarters, with analyst coverage 87.5% bullish and improving. The separation is the fix for the structural overhang rather than a new risk: Arkansas has barred pharmacy benefit managers from owning pharmacies and Tennessee has passed a similar law, and CVS own filing warns those laws limit its ability to offer both under one roof. Splitting the retail estate from Aetna and Caremark removes the conflict the legislation targets, and the 8-K says the separation is intended to be tax-free to shareholders. A 13x multiple on 8.33 of trailing earnings is 108, which is not a new high — the stock traded at 110.68 within the last 200 days and its 50-day and 200-day sit at 90.56 and 88.89. Downside case for the reward-to-risk is 68, roughly 8.2x and below the 69.51 200-day low.
key_risk: INVALIDATION (no hard stop, long-term): federal PBM legislation that materially resets Caremark economics, or two consecutive quarters of adjusted EPS below the consensus the company has beaten four straight times, or abandonment of the separation. A price move alone is not invalidation — at 9.8x the price is the opportunity. The live risks: PBM legislation bears directly on Caremark, the profit engine that stays with Aetna after the split; execution of a breakup announced for 2028 means two years of distraction, stranded corporate cost and the routine slippage large separations suffer; and insider data gives no confirmation, with zero open-market purchases against nine sales worth $359.0M over six months.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that a company announcing a breakup is admitting the integrated model failed, and that the market marked it down 12.5% for exactly that reason while peers rose (ELV +4%, CI +3%). Answered with the statute rather than with optimism: the integrated model is being made illegal state by state, Arkansas first and Tennessee behind it, so separation is not a confession of strategic failure but compliance arriving ahead of the mandate, and it converts a regulatory discount into two cleanly valued businesses.

catalyst.action: hold; move the stop to 103.20, just above the 103.00 entry and below the 104.04/104.99 moving-average shelf. Take the target at 117.34 if it trades there

thesis: This amends the exits on the open 2026-10-12 long at 103.00; the entry is filled and does not move. ABT closed 113.60, up 10.3% on the position and 3.3% below the 117.34 target, and it is only 3.19% off its 117.34 200-day high — the target is the high. The standing 97.00 stop is 16.60 below the market, 4.69 ATR on a 3.54 ATR, which means a winning position is still underwriting a 14.6% loss it no longer needs to carry. 103.20 sits 2.94 ATR below price, above the entry, and below the 50-day at 104.04 and the 20-day at 104.99, so it is a structural level rather than a round number. Healthcare was the defensive winner of the 2026-11-05 crash, with XLV down 2.50% against SPY down 4.41%, and ABT held better than the index on the day at -1.65%.
key_risk: Raising a stop to just above the entry on a name 3.3% from its target invites being shaken out of the last leg: 103.20 is 2.94 ATR away, which is a real buffer, but a single 9% medtech gap on a guidance revision clears it and the trade ends flat instead of at target. The honest trade-off is giving up the tail in exchange for guaranteeing the position cannot become a loss.
counter_argument: The case for simply taking the 10.3% now is that the target is the 200-day high and round-tripping a double-digit gain is the most common way a good trade becomes a bad one. The reason not to: the stop at 103.20 already makes that outcome impossible, so holding costs nothing but the spread between breakeven and 113.60 in the worst case, against 3.3% of upside in the best.
